turns.speaker: customer
turns.text: I don't actually have a part number. I was hoping you could help me figure out which one I need.

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: I can't really guess for you. If you don't have the part number, just check the website.

turns.speaker: customer
turns.text: Okay. Do you at least know if the 2-inch stainless one is in stock?

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: Probably. I'd have to go look. Hold on.

turns.speaker: customer
turns.text: Sure, I can wait. And while you're checking, how much is it and how fast can you ship it?

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: It's whatever the site says, and shipping takes however long it takes. I don't control that.

turns.speaker: customer
turns.text: All right. Can I just place the order with you over the phone?

turns.speaker: agent
turns.text: You can, but honestly, it's faster if you just do it online yourself. Is there anything else? I've got other calls waiting.

turns.speaker: customer
turns.text: No. No, I guess that's it.

Scorecard

Empathy 1/5 No acknowledgment of the customer's situation at any point. Responses are curt and dismissive rather than helpful, and the agent implies impatience instead of reassurance.
Communication 2/5 Answers are understandable but minimal and non-committal — no explanation, no next steps offered, nothing confirmed in concrete terms.
Professionalism 2/5 Not overtly hostile, but repeatedly blunt to the point of sounding annoyed, and steers the customer away from doing business over the phone.

Issue Resolution 1/5 Call ends with no part identified, no confirmed stock, no price, no shipping estimate, and no order placed — every question the customer asked was deflected.

What went well

  • Stayed on the call — Despite the customer not having a part number, the agent kept responding to each question rather than cutting the call short.
  • Didn't invent an answer — The agent avoided guessing at exact stock or price rather than telling the customer something that might be wrong.

What to work on

  • Offer to look up the part instead of sending the customer away — "2-inch stainless ball valve for a water line" is enough to search a catalog. Redirecting the customer to do that work themselves loses the sale and the relationship.
    Instead of: "I can't really guess for you. If you don't have the part number, just check the website."
    Try: "No problem — let me pull up 2-inch stainless ball valves for water line service and we'll find the right one together."
  • Confirm stock, price, and shipping before answering — Saying "probably" and "whatever the site says" gives the customer nothing to act on and makes the company look disorganized.
    Instead of: "It's whatever the site says, and shipping takes however long it takes. I don't control that."
    Try: "Let me check right now — I can give you the exact price and ship date before we hang up."
  • Don't discourage the customer from buying on the call — Telling a ready buyer it's "faster" to order online themselves, right after mentioning other calls waiting, reads as wanting to get off the phone rather than close the sale.
    Instead of: "You can, but honestly, it's faster if you just do it online yourself. Is there anything else? I've got other calls waiting."
    Try: "Absolutely, I can place that order for you right now — let's get it done."

One thing to practice before your next call

Before your next call, practice this response for when a customer doesn't have a part number: offer to look it up with them using what they describe, instead of sending them to find it themselves.
